blocks.x: Okay. How about you giving me your right name?
My right name is Leon René. Leon Theophilus René, if you want to. Theophilus? Theophilus.
That's my uncle's name.
T-H-E-L-U-S.

And I have a nephew name. That's all. Theophilus. Well, when my uncle was born, his father saw him and said, that's Theophilus-looking baby Alba. No, my uncle was the in man. Yeah, yeah. And so he always had bad jokes. Let's get your date back.
Is he going to talk over here?
Yeah, he should. Yeah, he should.
This is Googie René here. Better known as Rayfield Googie René.
And you're all a friend, son. You've known each other for a number of years.
A couple of years. Father and son. Father and son, that's right.
Googie is the son. And I'm Dick Allen. Real name Richard Benyon Allen. Now that we're confessing on a medical truth.
Richard Benyon Allen. I didn't know that. That's the one on me, that middle one.
Well, I think it must have been a French name or something.
Benyon. I never heard of that one.
Yeah. Anyway, we were looking at that picture of Buddy Petit. I sure would like to know more about Buddy Petit and what he played and what he sounded like.

Well, I don't know. First time that Buddy Petit came to Covington, I remember that very well. Because it probably was a Saturday night dance he had to play for. And so he did, he had to play this for, it was a white dance that was down in the Pavilion, that I recall, down by the river, Bofilaya River. And he got off the train and seated this customer at that time, naturally, for the band to play something at the station. You know, and we, so that everybody in town could know. It's just like broadcasting that I'm in town, that the dance will be held so the people could come. And so he blew some tunes down there that was out of this world. I'll never forget it because I heard it several blocks off, about maybe six or seven, eight blocks. You could, you know, it traveled, you know, those trumpets playing at night like that in the country town. So I ran down the station, that Buddy Petit was playing, you know, New Orleans jazz. Nothing in the country, that was just the greatest thing in the world, something to come into town like that, especially to give a dance. Now, I want to find out where the dance is, and probably everybody in town would be around the hall. That's what probably happened. And so we all actually listened a while, and when the band went to play at that particular dance, and then never mind, people would stand around, around the outside, a distance from the band, and listen to the music all night long. And he was a great, great band. And of course, later on, he was going to stay there for a while and play that territory for the summer. And of course, they told him that I was a piano player. And he said, come on down to Southern Hotel, and I'll see what you can play, what you know. So I went down to Southern Hotel, and he had a dance he was playing on there, and I played a few bars on the piano with him, the blues he was playing, which was easy. And he liked the way I was playing. He said, boy, you play all right. He said, I think I can use you. He said, I'll give you $3 a night. I think it was $3 a night or $3 a week. I'm not sure. But whatever it was, I never did get it. I think he gave me half of the amount. And I worked all summer, and I was so glad to work with his band. I didn't care whether they paid me or not. So that was kind of introduction to Buddy P.T. And that picture you see in the field. We played in Mandeville. And of course, there was nobody in the hall, and they said, they're going to take a picture of the band. Boy, come on out here. And I said, well, I can't. I play the piano. He said, well, you can't bring the piano. Pick something up and put it in your hand. Take that megaphone there and bring it on out there. So I had a cap on. I took the cap, put it on. I had my cap and I put it down. My eyes went out in that hot sun out in the middle of the field. And they took the picture. And I didn't realize when I took that picture that that picture would come back to be, not to haunt me so much, as to be a classic in the jazz field. Because Buddy P.T. was one of the greats. Yeah. And he, when I saw that picture in Hollywood, when I made success in my record company, exclusive records had arrived. And we had Joe Liggins and his Honey Drippers, the number one all over the country, right during the Louis Jordan area. And we were making money like mad with the $1.05 record. And I was getting my suits made at Cy DeVoza all across the street and sailing pretty high. And so I said, look at this. I see, I saw your picture in the Esquire. Well, I thought maybe it was going to find pictures, going to show me Esquire. And show me this Buddy P.T. picture of the old jazz guys. And he said, that's you with that funny hat on your head, cap on your head. I said, no, that's not me. He said, well, that looks like you. It surely looks like you. I thought it was going to disgrace me. You know, I said, this guy, wait a minute. I was thinking. And so I said, ah, sure, that's you. So I looked and I looked and I looked and I said, well, that might be me. I remember praying with Buddy. He said, sure, that's you. I said, I think that is me. And that's when I saw that picture for the first time. And it was in Esquire, all year, all jazz greats. I think Louis Armstrong's picture was in there. Buddy, all of us pictures on the first page.
We really got ahead. But because I should ask you when you were born and where and about your family and all that stuff.

Well, I was born in Covington, Louisiana. My mother, my father was a contractor in New Orleans. And when my mother took sick with tuberculosis, they had to move to the ozone belt. That was Covington. Because of the pine trees and the good weather over there, that was best to get well. And so I was born in Covington in 1902. And I was born on Florida Street. 7, 10 Florida Street. We tried to find it the other day when we went through. Couldn't find it. The house was toned down. But we saw an old store where we used to buy grocers. Miss Joe's. And we used to go down to Miss Joe's and get oil sausage and get anything you want that was in a barrel or whatever they were selling it. But the old place was just a regular little shanty. But it was up and still there after all these years. That must have been since 1910 that I remember. That's a long time. When I was a kid, you know, to remember going to the store. And so that's what I meant. I was born in Boston. I went to school there for a little while. But my dad was finished at Southern University and he naturally wanted, he was a contractor. And my mother played the piano and he played the violin. And he was a bricklayer contractor, bricklayer. And he played the violin as best he could, you know, with those bricklayer hands. But they used to play well together, as I remember. And I guess I took something that, some of the musical qualities from my mother and father. And it stuck with me through the years. I picked it up and started playing by ear. But that is something about Covington. Because my dad stayed there for years because of my mother's health until we moved to California.
I never told you, but my father was born on February the 6th. And you didn't say what day you were born.
I was born on February the 6th, 1902.
You told me the year, but not the day. It's the same thing as my father was born.
February the 6th, 1902. Isn't that something? Yeah.
That's a funny coincidence. But, yeah. Did your father study any mathematics or anything like that?
Yes.
Did you know much about that sort of stuff?

Yes. My dad was finished, the highest in his class in mathematics. And that's one reason why they thought that when he was in school, they wanted him to become a teacher at Southern because of his high marks in mathematics. But he decided he wanted to be a contractor, and a mason, you know, contractor. So he decided to go into that. And so he started here on the apprenticeship. I don't know who he worked on the apprenticeship of, but he worked here. And he became very good and started drawing plans and his own plans and working with some contractor until he became so good that when he went to Covenant, he became his own man. And he became a contractor. And it was a brick base, not a general contract, but in there. And he built several buildings over there. School, high school was built there. It was at that time, it was a white high school. And it was a southern hotel, which was a block long. The high school took a whole square, four blocks. And a depot there, where the New Orleans Great Northern came in from New Orleans every day. From New Orleans, and that was the excitement then. Those days, an excursion on Sundays that came from New Orleans to Covenant for a dollar. Round trip. That was part of the, his whole life was dedicated to being a contractor. And he started his contracting business from Covenant and eventually moved to California.
Do you remember about the square of the hypotenuse and all those stories?

Oh, yeah. The square of the hypotenuse. Papa had a building to build, had a gymnasium to build at St. John's Academy. I think it was St. John's Academy. In Covington. A Catholic institution, college. And Papa had the building, had New Orleans bricklayers over there. And Faberick and Liberty was the architects, greatest architects in the South. And they drew the plans to this octagon building. All the brickwork was octagon. And they had it all laid out and everything. And so the building, they got up about four feet with the building. And Papa came there and said, took some measurements around and started to figure in something. And it stopped the job. And he said, wait a minute. I said, we're not going any further. There's something wrong here. He looked at the plans. And he says, let me see something. And so he went up to the dean of the college in the mathematics, I guess, department at that time. And he said, something's wrong with this plan. It's not correct because we're running into trouble. But when they get up to the roof, this dome that they're going to put on this gymnasium is not going to fit. And so he was right in the room with all these students, trigonometry and so forth, and geometry and whatever it was, the class. And they all laughed at it. They said it wouldn't fit. So they said, well, Rene, what do you think Fabian Livet-Date should do about this? They were making a fool out of it, trying to make a fool out of the old man. And so I said, my dad, and so I said, he said, well, I said, he said, no, he says, no, it's nothing of a laughing matter. It's a thing that's going to cost you a lot of money. He says, the building is going up and it's not going to be within the framework. The brickwork is not going to be matched. The dome is coming in. And it's going to be expensive. You're going to have to tear it down. So they laughed. They said, why is it you're going to tear it down? It's a simple rule there. You should know that. And an octagon, and he told them the rule of the, I can't remember how exactly the rule. It's the regular rule.
It was the square of the hypotenuse.
Yes, that's right. Square of the hypotenuse.
That's what I remember from three years.

That's right. That's right. Sum of the square of the side. That's right. Square of the side. And that's the thing. When he said that, then the whole school says, hey, wait, let's see. And then after they found out that he was right, they were surprised. And boy, did their faces turn red to find that they were laughing at him, something with a simple rule that they should have known. And then they sent for Faberick and Liberty to come over there immediately. And he came up on a Sunday on a train, excursion train, and checked his plans. And he said to Papa, he says, we're going to reward you with something, quite an extra amount of money that they paid him for it. He said, you saved us thousands of dollars, because that would have definitely been expensive for us. So he was highly respected after that. He was considered one of the finest mathematicians and contractors in that area.
He said, you know, I love those stories like that. They tell you a lot about it.
Yes, they do.
You don't have to worry about the mic. We can just relax and talk to each other.
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
He's picking you up fine.
Did he finish about the hypotheses?
Yeah. Yeah.
I'll fix it. While you were asleep. Yeah, that's true. Looks tired.
Anyway, what kind of music did they play together, your mother and father?

Well, let me see. They played the operas. Mama sang a few of the light operas, you know, the operas of that day that came to the French opera house, you know, some of the great operas that Papa had the music. Mama had the music. She played the Romeo, not Romeo, but the... She된 stuff.

one that goes, I can't think of the names, it's a funny thing, all of the Italian operas that you, I can't think of, some of the, I don't say them often, and that's what sometimes you forget them, but anyhow, all of the great operas that came to the French opera, naturally they all came from Paris, all these operas, and they didn't come from any of the United States, from New York, they came from Paris, and they played at the French opera house, and when they played at the French opera house, everybody went, Mama used to always go, and Papa did too, and they loved opera, and they learned all of the operas, and all of the famous operas of that time, and it was generally, good music at that time was encouraged, and they played it, and sang it, and parties instead, at least Mama did, and Papa too, and that was a way of entertaining, I never forget Mama, she was at a Baptist church, some friends of hers invited her over to a concert, and she went over, and she was singing one of her songs, and she was playing it, and all of a sudden, she got to a certain part in it, and she forgot all the words, and everything, she just stopped and took a bow, and went off, no one knew, I said, why did Mama go off so suddenly, she just forgot the words, and no one knew that she didn't know the rest of the song.
Were you raised a Baptist?

The old Catholic, I was raised a Catholic, and that's the time when the Catholic, I never forget my mother and father at that time, my grandfather was named Bowman, he was shipping commissioner here, what I meant, he had his charge of all the boats that came in from South America, those fruit boats that brought bananas and all the things, all the boats that came in, and they had to go to his office to get okay, and he was well off, there was quite a story behind him before he came to New Orleans, because he was just formerly from Germany, Grandpa Bowman, and he had his home with his children, 11 children, with my grandmother, who was a mother, who was, at that time, she was colored at that time, between colored and part Indian, and she, naturally, they live on Lyon Street, and he was doing very well, one of his, two of his sons were in the post office, and so forth, so they did very well, so Grandpa was the, well, let's see, what was I saying, I was trying to figure out what the plan was, I was talking about, what was I saying? I was talking about your religion. Oh, my religion, yes, and so, so, my dad was kind of, as he saw, but he has kind of a Roman nose like I have, to someone, but he was dark brown skinned, his dad was French, René, his name René, and he was chef, cooked at the St. Charles Hotel, here, chef pastry cook, and so, Papa was allowed to court Mama, although the Mama and the family of the Bowmans were very light-complected, you know, and some of them were, even when, you know, Pastor White, you might say, it was there, you were on the other side, some of them, and, but, she was allowed to come to the house and eventually married Mama. He was, Mama was much older than yours, maybe about five or six years or so, or more, and they, they got married, and, and when he got married, there's this church there on Napoleon, Napoleon and Camp Street called, what was that, St. St. David, I can't, you find the name. We can ride by it, maybe. Yes, the St. David.
I can bum a ride with you.

Yes, that's right, yes, we have, right on the corner, that particular, right across from McDonough 6 school, and the Bowmans always had pews way up in front of the church, but when Papa, Mama married Papa, he was dark, brown skinned, and the ushers would, came up to Papa, and asked him to please be seated in the rear of the church, because that they had reservations for colored people to sit in the back of the church, that time they had a little sign for colored only, back there, see, for colored patrons only. So, Mama said, you sit right here, and they said he came back two, three times, and so Papa, Mama said, don't you move, you stay right here, because that was the family pew up there, two, three of them, two peributes, and so, he didn't move, so, after that, they got, after church was over, he came up to Papa, and he says, said something about, he shouldn't sit in that part of the church before, again, because that was reserved for whites, and so, they took Grandpa and his family, just for whites, they'd understood that's where it was, and so Mama decided from then on, she didn't want to go to church anymore, she, although we were Catholic, and we were born Catholic, we were trade men, and not until she went to California did she start to go into church again, because the same thing happened in Covington, the same thing, because of the fact they isolated the Catholics to the the fact that they would, the colors would sit in the back, and but the communion time, you could go up together, and sit after the, after the whites people had received communion, and this was something, in those days, it doesn't happen today, you understand, but this thing there, they, and after they received communion, you would receive communion, that was something that the church itself tolerated because of the law, you see, and that they, while the church, they closed the church down, and that's one of the reasons why the church was a fear for the law, closing down the church, so there was, so, I mean, the church was fearful of the law, closing down, so they, they had to abide by that law, so from two later years, when they fought that off, but there's a religion, there's Catholic, that's what was, and did you ever go to a Catholic school? No, I, I went to, in Covington, in Covington, no, there wasn't any, you see, there never was, at that time, the Catholics did not take in any, uh, color that told at that time, they didn't take anybody in there, other than, uh, they, in fact, they had a school for girls, uh, but it was only for, uh, white girls, and so forth, but not for colored black girls, or anything like that, they, at that time, that was way back now, you ever say, way back in, when segregation was, was tolerated, and so forth, you know, times of the day. Oh, yeah. See, that was, I remember. This was way back in the old days, but it took, uh, it got to change, the church changed all that, you know, as time went on, and of course, it's, uh, the laws became, uh, you know, different, at least all this, uh, the, uh, civil rights, and so forth, movement, so forth, changed, all these things, and everything opened up, and it's changed everything, but, but, uh, no one could fight that law, because it's separate, but equal, because it was definitely something that, uh, in fact, it happened during the time, uh, right on the New Orleans Great Northern train going to Covington, you see, Plessy versus New Orleans Great, huh? Ferguson, Plessy, was it Plessy? Plessy versus Ferguson, I remember it. Ferguson, yeah, yeah, yeah. On the New Orleans Great Northern, on the New Orleans Great Northern Red Road. I don't remember it too well. The judge in the Supreme Court, as a separate but equal would be all right, and that's what, until that was, uh, outlawed, and voted down in the Supreme Court years later. What, did you get any musical training in Covington? Well, my mother, I just took the musical, and played by ear, played by ear, and, uh, played by ear, but I was good at it. You see, when you play by ear, it's just like Cookie did. You go, you get out and you can develop well, it's like a lot of the jazz musicians today. You play by ear, you, you, you can do a lot of things that you invent, you see, it have to be a composing in years to come. So, uh, I would play piano, and make up the songs, and, as I heard them, uh, uh, played around, or, you know, records, and you'd hear them blasting out of people's houses. You can hear records in those old days, Mamie Smith records, and you could hear all the old, Tony O'Neill, Ted Lewis records, you know. You could hear all the old, you could hear all the, you could hear all the, you could hear all the, you could hear that same tune all day. So that you'd learn it, and eventually play it. See, I never bought any, because I'd just listen, and then I learned how to play it. But it was soon, so then I got a job playing at the theater, at the colored picture show, because the guy played down there, he played down there. He played nothing but boogie woogie all through the love scenes. So they didn't want him in there, because he messed up the love scenes with boogie woogie. That's all he played stuff with boogie woogie. That's all he played. So they say Doc played a little different stuff with stuff I was composing, didn't know it. Horses would bloom, so I'd make some kind of horse music. If there was anything, they were shooting at one another, I'd make some kind of a, you know, sort of a radical sort of a overture or something, like it was going to have a war going on, and I would do it with my, just originally. But the funniest thing that I had noticed, they would sometimes, when they'd come down to the color house, they'd bring the fourth reel first, you see, then they'd start to come back again. They couldn't let them have the other reel, so they'd send the second reel. Now you have to put that together, what the story was about, because they started with the fourth reel, now it's the second reel, then they come back with the fifth reel, that five reels, you know, then you come back maybe with the third reel, and then the first reel, and you put it all together, and you figure out what kind of show. But so that's what, so one time, it was there, and the old guys, the films caught on fire, and you see what I mean, and the, and the guys had buckets of water was coming in, and put the film out, they couldn't get the film back to the white picture show, because they'd switch them, see, the same guy, finally, owned the white picture show, and the black picture show. So he was sending one film down there, while he'd pick up the other one, bring them down there, and he had them switching, so he could have one film playing two houses. And that's what happened. And later on he gave me a, he said, what do you call it, I got transferred to the other theater, and then they paid me a dollar more a week, to the white theater, until it came the four horsemen of the apocalypse, I think it was, and they had the music with it, had to read. I couldn't read that hard music that came with the score, and so, and so they had to finally get some piano player from Yale to play the piano, for the score that was, that hard score that was coming. That was changing, and coming in sound was coming. But that's why I got a lot of experience in writing, and making up songs, and might have helped me later on in the poetry.
How much did you get a week ordinarily?
A dollar and a half a week. A dollar and a half.
And then when you went to the white theater, you got...
Got two dollars and a half. Oh, that was a big raise. I got a big raise. Oh yeah, that would be.
Yeah.

A dollar and a half. Two and a half. And I was, I was glad to get that. And of course there was no one to take my place down at the other, I think they got the other Boogie Wiggy, Boogie Wiggy Plow, and he got his job back. And they never did like him, because he played with, when they played the scenes of the comedy, you know, he was all right with the Boogie Wiggy. Then they went into the love scenes, where when they played love scenes, it's supposed to be sweet and he was playing Boogie Wiggy all the time.
Did you know his name?
Slim something, I don't know if that was his name. Slim, he was a tall guy, Slim, Slim Jackson, or something like that. Slim Jackson, I think that was his name.
Yeah, of course there were quite a few musicians around coming.
He wasn't, he was no musician. He was, he was a honky-ton piano player.
Yeah, but I mean they had guys that could play over there anyway.
No, no, there wasn't nobody. I was the only one in the town that played.
Piano.
Yes, and I, they were high for the party.
Yeah, but they had other people around, didn't they, some time to time?
Nobody. Playing horns? No, no.
Not the fritzes weren't around?

No horn players, no, no. That's why when Buddy P.T. came to town, they got, you know, they were considered like, you know, celebrities, you know, after all coming to town. With jazz, you know, music like that, you know, those fellas were supposed to be, boy they were really worshipped, especially coming to the station to play. And everybody in town would come down to the station, just to get and play. It was, it was a scene. It's like TV, it's greater than TV is today for them at that time.
Mm-hmm, sure. Let me get a little bit real loud. But, uh, was Buddy a straight trumpet player or could he play variations?
Yes, Buddy a straight track, but he was a, Buddy was a kind of a rock, he rocked on that melody line. He took the melody line and that trombone player, uh, what's his name?
The one in the picture?
Yeah, well, I can't, what's that?
George Washington.

George, yeah. George Washington played, uh, uh, right with him. It was the best trumpet and trombone team in New Orleans at that time. The two, for teaming. Now he didn't play the high notes so much. He didn't go up for the screaming high notes like Kid Renee and some of the bands at that time. See, Louis had...

left I think to go to Chicago. These fellows were then taking over. Buddy had that smooth rocking style and George would kind of play along with him. And they came to California with that style. That was very good. They featured that. They didn't read music to that extent. Buddy could, but I understand that the trombone player could. So he had to go back to New Orleans when he went to Los Angeles. But in Covington, when they played. Buddy and I didn't go up to high notes, but it was mostly in that rock, I don't say rock, but I mean in that weaving sort of Dixie, New Orleans style. New Orleans style music. It was. He had a great sound in Clannad, but he had a great drummer. His drummer was the bass player. That was, you have to call him. Face up. Eddie Woods. Yeah, Eddie Woods. Eddie Woods was one of the greatest drummers. Believe me, that guy could play a tremendous beat. He was great. And so was the Clannadis, which was, uh, and, uh, Edmund Hall. Yeah, Edmund, and, and of course, uh, uh, Chester on bass. But that, and the guitar man, which was banjo, uh, which was, uh, his name had been, uh. Buddy Manatee, we were talking about. Buddy Manatee. And he, he had that, it was a combination of the whole band. They played solid to get stuff down at Preservation Hall when I was in 76, Chester was playing with bands and he began to play, because I was in there, like he used to play then. Chester's a great bass player, was playing that style that Buddy played at that time. And believe me, I got the greatest thrill at Preservation Hall listening to that band when he was playing. Because he sends that band with that bass. He plays a strong bass, slap bass as well as a full bass sound. He sends a band. And that band of Buddy P.T.'s was that kind of a band. They just was like together like, and when he bowed, they would see kind of a, had a feeling one pushing the other. Yeah. And that's.

Let's see if it's working. It seems to be. We got the second reel on now. For Leon Rene. Okay, we were talking about Buddy and all that and I, but uh, and I wanted to know if he did anything about harmony at all. Harmony? Harmony? Yeah. Uh, what do you mean though? Do you think he, had ever studied any harmony? Oh, you mean, you mean, had Buddy studied harmony? Studied harmony so he could. I don't think he did. He played from a natural sound.
He might have known, but he didn't. He did.
He did. He did. He did. He did. He did. He did.
He did. He did.
He did.

He did. He did. He did.
